title: Learning guitar from a friend named Lawrence, and playing Jim Canen
summary: At about ten he learned finger-style guitar and the blues from Lawrence, and plays a demonstration of Jim Canen with a modern ending.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Around about ten years old.
Uh-huh.
This was around about 1909 and I'm
always a year ahead of the year, see, in 1909 I'm ten, see. So I was about ten years old at that time.
Was it just a guitar around the house or was there a neighbor who played guitar?

It was a guitar around the house, but it was a friend of ours. His name was Lawrence. All I can remember is Lawrence, name -- I don't know his last name. But Lawrence and the first ting he taught me to play was Jim Canen, and also after he taught us the Jim Canen then he played the blues and we learned how to play the blues. And I still play those old blues yet. Blues that I played way back there when I was a boy around about nine or ten years old.
What were some of their names?
Well, all I know, Jim Canen. I don't know. Would you like to hear that Jim Canen?
Yes. uh-huh. Oh, you still play guitar.

Yes, uh-huh. I don't do too much of it now because -- just enough. Now, the Jim Canen was nothing but just -- we played finger style, which at time we called it the finger style, but it's the classic as I know, the classic, and it -- cause when you play with the pick (unintelligible) when you play with the fingers, it's pizicato, see.
Yes.
But I didn't know that at that time.
I didn't know pizzicato from (unintelligible) Now, here's the other thing
[Jim Canen]
(music)
Were you doing that ending when you were ten years old? That's a little modern touch that you added.

Well, unfortunately, I didn't know anything about that ending that I just did, because that ending entailed a C6, well, I didn't know anything about a C6. I just did it just to play an ending. Now, with the blues, whenever I would go in and all the men would be playing blues, they'd get up and say, 'Give Randolph the guitar,' see, because I'd have the blues and here I'd go.
(music)
Bet you didn't use that chord in 1909 either.
No, I didn't use that chord.
That was a pretty chord.
No, I didn't use that chord either, not that one.
That [Jim Canen] sounds like sort of a reel -- a folk dance number.
Well, I guess so. You know, the years takes a toll and, you know, I used to really could play that, being young and the dextrose of my fingers was really active
and I could play it very, very fast, but this time I haven't got that speed now.
Sure, I understand.
I'm 78 now, you know, different from a boy's fingers, ten year old kid's fingers and (then) a 78 --
Yeah.
Yeah, yes.
